sections.b: The Psalter ends with five psalms that each begin and end with hallelu-yah, which the site's Plain renders "Praise the LORD!": "Praise the LORD! / My soul, praise the LORD!" (Psalm 146:1). The praise widens from one soul to Jerusalem (147:12), to all creation (148), to the assembly of the loyal (149), and at last to everything alive: "Let every breathing thing praise Yah! / Praise the LORD!" (150:6). In the Greek the hallelujahs are moved into the headings, where three of these psalms are also credited to Haggai and Zechariah. In Jewish prayer Psalms 145–150 are said every morning, and the Talmud's wish to be among "those who complete the Hallel every day" is understood of them (Bavli Shabbat 118b, with Rashi).

sections.h: The end of the Psalter: Psalms 138–150
sections.b: Book V closes with a last collection headed "of David" (Psalms 138–145) and the final Hallel (146–150). In the David psalms the king prays to be searched and known (139), to be kept from slanderers and from his own evil words (140–141), cries from a cave (142), confesses that "no living person is in the right in your presence" (143:2), and asks for victory as a mere mortal, "a puff of air" (144:4). Then David himself praises God as King in the alphabet poem of Psalm 145, the only psalm called "a praise" (tehillah), whose plural became the Hebrew name of the book. The five closing psalms are all praise, and Psalm 150 serves as the doxology, the closing blessing of praise, of Book V and of the whole book. The Greek numbering, one behind since Psalm 10, catches up when it divides Psalm 147 in two, and then adds Psalm 151 "outside the number".
sections.refs: Psalm 139:1; Psalm 143:2; Psalm 144:4; Psalm 145:1; Psalm 147:12; Psalm 150:6

sections.b: Psalm 150 names more instruments than any other psalm: the ram's horn (shofar) blown by priests, the harp and lyre (nevel and kinnor) of the Levites, the tambourine or frame drum (tof) played by women at dances, strings (minnim), the reed pipe ('ugav, Jubal's instrument in Genesis 4:21), and two kinds of cymbals, those "that ring out" and the cymbals "of the loud shout" (150:5). The Greek renders the pipe as organon, and the Latin organum gave English the word "organ". Whether such instruments belong in Christian worship is debated; the Psalm 150 chapter page has a card on how the churches read it, and the 1 Chronicles 25 page another on David's musicians.

sections.h: "A hatred that holds nothing back": Psalms 139, 140 and 149
sections.b: The last psalms of the Psalter still contain curses. Psalm 139 turns from wonder at God's knowledge to "God, if only you would put the wicked to death!" (139:19) and "I hate them with a hatred that holds nothing back" (139:22), then asks God to search the singer himself (139:23–24). Psalm 140 asks for coals of fire on the slanderers (140:10). Psalm 149 gives the loyal "a double-edged sword in their hand, / to bring vengeance on the nations" (149:6–7). Churches often leave these lines out: the Revised Common Lectionary never appoints 139:19–22. Augustine read "perfect hatred" as hating sin while loving the sinner; Rashi read the sword of 149 as praise itself, and the Midrash on Psalms stresses that vengeance belongs to God. Delitzsch warned how a literal reading of Psalm 149 fed religious war in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Psalm 145 is said three times a day in the synagogue as Ashrei, introduced by Psalm 84:4 and 144:15 ("Happy is the people whose God is the LORD!") and closed with 115:18. The Talmud says that whoever says it three times a day may be sure of the world to come, because it is an alphabet psalm and because it contains "You open your hand / and fill every living thing with what it longs for" (145:16; Bavli Berakhot 4b). Psalms 146–150 follow it every morning. In the church, Psalms 148–150 closed Morning Prayer for more than a thousand years and gave the office of Lauds its name, and in the Byzantine rite they are the "Praises" of Matins.
sections.refs: Psalm 145:1–21; Psalm 144:15; Psalm 84:4; Psalm 115:18; Psalm 148:1; Psalm 150:6

sections.h: All creation called to praise: Psalm 148
sections.b: Psalm 148 calls on the heavens and the earth in an order like Genesis 1: angels and armies, sun, moon and stars, the waters over the heavens, then "you sea monsters and every ocean deep" (148:7), weather, mountains, trees, animals, birds, and finally every kind of human being. The creatures praise because "he gave the order, and they were created" (148:5). The Song of the Three Young Men in the Greek Daniel uses the same pattern, and Francis of Assisi's Canticle of the Creatures grew from both. Psalm 147 adds God who "counts how many stars there are" and gives the raven's chicks their food (147:4, 9).
sections.refs: Psalm 148:1–14; Genesis 1:1–31; Psalm 147:4; Psalm 147:9; Psalm 104:1–35; Revelation 5:13

sections.h: God the King at the close of the Psalter
sections.b: In the last psalm headed "of David", David himself calls God "my God, the King" (145:1) and praises his kingdom: "Your kingdom is a kingdom for all ages, / and your rule lasts through every generation" (145:13). The final Hallel repeats it: "The LORD will be king forever" (146:10), and Zion's children are to "celebrate their King" (149:2). Many scholars read this as the editors' answer to the fall of David's house lamented in Psalm 89: the human king bows to the divine King.
sections.refs: Psalm 145:1; Psalm 145:11–13; Psalm 146:10; Psalm 149:2; Psalm 89:38–51; Daniel 4:3

sections.h: "No living person is in the right": Psalm 143:2
sections.b: Psalm 143, the last of the seven Penitential Psalms, asks: "Do not go to trial with your servant, / for no living person is in the right in your presence" (143:2). Paul echoes the line in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16, adding "by works of the law". The psalm's remedy is God's own righteousness: "Answer me by your faithfulness, by your righteousness" (143:1). Luther counted it among the "Pauline psalms" for this reason.

"It was you who made my kidneys; / you wove me together in my mother's womb" (139:13). Psalm 139 pictures God forming a person before birth, seeing "a shapeless lump" and writing its days in his scroll (139:16). The Catholic Catechism cites the psalm with Jeremiah 1:5 for the dignity of human life from conception (Catechism 2270), and many Christians cite it in the debate over abortion; others answer that the poem praises God's knowledge and does not define when personhood begins. All readers agree that it places life before birth within God's care.

Besides the Egyptian Hallel (113–118) and the Great Hallel (136), Jewish tradition knows a third, said every day: the closing psalms of the Psalter, recited in the morning service (Pesukei de-Zimra). The Talmud has Rabbi Yose wish for his portion to be "with those who complete the Hallel every day", and the Talmud explains that this means the daily psalms of praise, since the festival Hallel may not be said every day; Rashi names Psalms 148 and 150 (Bavli Shabbat 118b). Psalms 146–150 each begin and end with "Praise the LORD!", and Psalm 145 (Ashrei) leads into them.
